etymology: The third-person singular present of seem, with the Old English -eth ending. Webster 1828: appeareth; hath the appearance of. The word marks appearance as distinguished from reality, which is exactly the distinction Proverbs 14:12 turns on.
biblical_def: Seemeth is the Bible’s word for how a thing looks, and Scripture uses it chiefly to warn that looking is not being. The most sobering use is repeated twice in Proverbs, once in each half of the book, as though the Spirit knew it needed saying again: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death (Proverbs 14:12), and again word for word at Proverbs 16:25. The road is not merely permitted to look right; it does look right, to the man walking it, and the appearance holds until the end. That is the whole doctrine of self-deception in a sentence. But the word also has a submissive use, where a man surrenders judgment to a higher authority. Eli, told that his house is ruined and that no sacrifice will purge it, answers, It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good (1 Samuel 3:18). The Gibeonites, caught in their deception and standing in Joshua’s hand, say the same: as it seemeth good and right unto thee to do unto us, do (Joshua 9:25). Between those two uses lies the whole practical question of the Christian life: whether what seems right to me governs, or what seems good to God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives SEEMETH as the third person singular of the verb seem: to appear; to make or have a show; to have the semblance, whether real or not. Webster notes that the word properly expresses appearance and therefore admits of a contrast with the thing itself.
webster_full: SEEMETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb SEEM.
SEEM, v.i. — To appear; to make or have a show or semblance.
To have the appearance of truth or fact; to be understood as true, though it may not be so.
It seemeth good — a phrase expressing what appears fit, right, or pleasing to a person in authority.
From Saxon seman, to satisfy or compose — connected with seemly, that which appears becoming.
scriptures: Proverbs 14:12
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
Proverbs 16:25
There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
1 Samuel 3:18
And Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him. And he said, It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.
Joshua 9:25
And now, behold, we are in thine hand: as it seemeth good and right unto thee to do unto us, do.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 14:12 denies exactly what the modern conscience assumes — that sincerity secures a man, and that a path which seems right to the one walking it cannot be the road to death.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is repeated in Proverbs precisely because the error is so durable. It does not say that the wicked man knows he is wicked and proceeds anyway; it says the way seemeth right, which means the traveller has examined his conscience and been satisfied. Sincerity is therefore no evidence of safety, and the modern maxim that a person must follow his own truth is the exact proposition Solomon warns against. Jeremiah adds the reason: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? (Jeremiah 17:9). A faculty that is itself corrupted cannot be the final court on its own condition, which is why Scripture, not the inner sense of rightness, is the standard.

Eli’s response gives the antidote, and it is bracing rather than comforting. He has just heard that his house will be judged for ever for a sin he knew of and did not restrain, and he answers, It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good. That is not resignation; it is the submission of a man who accepts God’s appraisal of his family over his own. Where the modern instinct asks whether a verdict feels fair, Eli asks only whose verdict it is. The dictionary does not present this as a hard saying to be softened: what seems right to a man is not the measure of anything, and what seems good to God is the measure of everything.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashar (H3477), straight, right, upright — right in a man’s own eyes; tob (H2896), good; Greek dokeo (G1380), to seem, to think, to suppose; phainomai (G5316), to appear.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, upright, right; the word behind seemeth right and behind every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Judges 21:25).
Hebrew tob (H2896) — good, pleasing; let him do what seemeth him good (1 Samuel 3:18).
Greek dokeo (G1380) — to seem, to suppose; the root of doxa in its older sense of opinion, and of docetism, the heresy that Christ only seemed to have a body.
Greek phainomai (G5316) — to appear, to be manifest; used of the whited sepulchres that appear beautiful outward (Matthew 23:27).
Greek eudokeo (G2106) — to think well of, to be well pleased; the New Testament’s it seemed good in Acts 15:28.
usage: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man (Proverbs 14:12) — sincerity is no evidence of safety.
Let him do what seemeth him good (1 Samuel 3:18) — submission to a verdict against one’s own house.
As it seemeth good and right unto thee to do unto us, do (Joshua 9:25) — men who have forfeited every claim.

etymology: The third-person singular present of proceed, from Latin procedere, to go forward, from pro (forward) and cedere (to go). Webster 1828: goeth forth; issueth; cometh from as a source. In theology the word is technical: the Spirit proceedeth from the Father.
biblical_def: Proceedeth names a going-forth from a source, and Scripture uses it of three things — the word of God, the speech of men, and the Person of the Holy Spirit. Of the word: man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live (Deuteronomy 8:3), which the Lord Jesus quoted to Satan in the wilderness in the form by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). The manna and the word are set together: God fed Israel with bread they had not sown to teach them that the real sustenance was His speech. Of men’s speech, James exposes the contradiction: Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be (James 3:10) — one spring cannot honestly yield two waters. Ecclesiastes notes that evil can proceed from a throne: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceedeth from the ruler (Ecclesiastes 10:5). Highest of all is the Trinitarian use: even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me (John 15:26). The Spirit’s procession is eternal and personal, not an event in time, and the clause is one of the pillars of the doctrine of the Trinity.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives PROCEEDETH as the third person singular of PROCEED: to move, pass, or go forward from one place or stage to another; to issue or come forth, as from a source, cause, or fountain.
webster_full: PROCEEDETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb PROCEED.
PROCEED, v.i. — To move, pass, or go forward from one place, point, or stage to another.
To issue or come forth, as from a source or fountain; as, light proceeds from the sun.
To be produced or propagated by; to result from as an effect from its cause.
From Latin pro, forward, and cedo, to go — the root also of process, procession, and precede.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 8:3

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
Matthew 4:4
But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.
James 3:10
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
Ecclesiastes 10:5
There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceedeth from the ruler:
corruption_summary: John 15:26 is the verse behind the greatest division in church history, and the dictionary holds the Western reading: the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, the filioque that the East rejected in 1054 and rejects still.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed of 381 said the Spirit proceeds from the Father; the Western church added filioque, and from the Son, first in Spain and eventually at Rome, and the East treated the addition as both unauthorised and false. The dictionary affirms the filioque on scriptural grounds. The Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9) and the Spirit of his Son (Galatians 4:6); the risen Lord breathed on the disciples and said Receive ye the Holy Ghost; and John 15:26 itself has Christ sending the Comforter — whom I will send unto you from the Father — in the same clause that names the procession. The Reformed confessions carry the Western doctrine, and the 1689 follows Westminster in affirming it.

The second corruption concerns the first two verses rather than the fourth. Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4 are routinely quoted to mean that spiritual things matter more than material ones, which is true but is not what either text says. Israel was hungry because God made them hungry, fed with a bread they did not recognise, in order to teach that His word is what sustains life. Christ quoted it to a tempter urging Him to make bread, and the point was obedience to a Father who had led Him into the wilderness and not yet fed Him. James 3:10 supplies the practical corollary about our own mouths: the tongue that blesses God on Sunday and curses men made in His likeness the rest of the week has not two sources but one, and James refuses to let the contradiction stand.
roots_summary: Greek ekporeuomai (G1607), to go forth out of, the verb of John 15:26; proerchomai (G4281), to go before; Hebrew motsa (H4161), a going forth, an utterance; yatsa (H3318), to go out.
roots_lines: Greek ekporeuomai (G1607) — to go forth out of; the technical verb of the Spirit’s procession (John 15:26) and of words out of the mouth (Matthew 4:4).
Hebrew motsa (H4161) — a going forth, that which issues; every word that proceedeth in Deuteronomy 8:3 is literally every motsa of the mouth of the LORD.
Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, to come forth; the root of motsa.
Greek pege (G4077) — a spring, a fountain; James 3:11 asks whether a pege sends forth sweet water and bitter.
Greek rhema (G4487) — a spoken word, an utterance; the word that proceeds out of the mouth of God in Matthew 4:4.
usage: Every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD (Deuteronomy 8:3) — the word, not the bread, is what sustains.
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing (James 3:10) — one spring cannot honestly yield two waters.
The Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father (John 15:26) — the eternal procession, and the ground of the filioque.

etymology: The third-person singular present of stir, from Saxon styrian, to move, to agitate. Webster 1828: moveth; agitateth; exciteth. Scripture uses it of an eagle rousing her young, of a proud heart raising strife, and of hell itself roused to meet a fallen king.
biblical_def: Stirreth is a word of rousing, and Scripture applies it to God’s care, to man’s pride, and to the grave. The tenderest use is God’s own picture of how He taught Israel: As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings (Deuteronomy 32:11). The nest is broken up deliberately so that the eaglets will fly, and the same wings that disturb them catch them. That is the shape of God’s hard providences toward His people: the comfortable place is unsettled by the One who intends to carry them. Proverbs uses the word twice of what a bad heart produces: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins (Proverbs 10:12), and He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the LORD shall be made fat (Proverbs 28:25). In both, strife is not an accident of circumstance but the output of a settled disposition. And Isaiah gives the word its most terrible use, as the grave rouses its inhabitants to greet the king of Babylon: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth (Isaiah 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives STIRRETH as the third person singular of STIR: to move; to agitate; to bring into debate or action; to incite, instigate, or excite, as to stir up strife or to stir up the mind.
webster_full: STIRRETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb STIR.
STIR, v.t. — To move; to change place in any manner; to agitate what is at rest.
To incite to action; to instigate; to prompt; as, to stir up a people to rebellion.
To excite or raise; as, to stir up strife, contention, or the affections.
From Saxon styrian, to move — connected with storm and with stern in its older sense of stirring or violent.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:11
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:
Proverbs 10:12
Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
Proverbs 28:25
He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the LORD shall be made fat.
Isaiah 14:9

Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations.
corruption_summary: Proverbs traces strife to a proud heart in the man who raises it, and the modern habit of explaining conflict entirely by circumstance, systems, or the other party’s behaviour removes the one cause Scripture actually names.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 10:12 and 28:25 both put the cause inside the man: hatred stirs up strifes; a proud heart stirs up strife. James asks the same question and gives the same answer — From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? (James 4:1). Against that stands the now-dominant habit of accounting for conflict by structures, personality types, communication styles, or the wounds a person carries, all of which may be genuinely present and none of which is the biblical diagnosis. The practical consequence is enormous: if strife proceeds from pride in me, then the first move in every quarrel is repentance, and I can make it without waiting for the other party. If strife proceeds from circumstance, I must wait for the circumstance to change, and I usually wait for ever.

Deuteronomy 32:11 corrects a corruption of the opposite kind — the assumption that a settled, comfortable life is the mark of God’s favour. The eagle deliberately breaks up the nest. The disturbance is not the withdrawal of care but its exercise, and the wings that unsettle are the wings that bear. Read against Isaiah 14:9, where hell itself is stirred up to receive a man who exalted himself, the two uses frame the alternative plainly: God stirs His people out of comfort in order to carry them, and the proud man stirs up strife until the grave stirs to meet him.
roots_summary: Hebrew ur (H5782), to rouse, to awake, to stir up; garah (H1624), to stir up strife, to contend; Greek diegeiro (G1326), to arouse thoroughly; anazopureo (G329), to stir into flame.
roots_lines: Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, to awake; the eagle stirring her nest (Deuteronomy 32:11) and hell stirring the dead (Isaiah 14:9).
Hebrew garah (H1624) — to stir up, to contend, to meddle; hatred stirreth up strifes (Proverbs 10:12).
Hebrew madon (H4066) — strife, contention; the noun that garah produces in Proverbs 28:25.
Greek diegeiro (G1326) — to arouse completely; Peter stirs up his readers by putting you in remembrance (2 Peter 1:13).
Greek anazopureo (G329) — to rekindle, to fan into flame; stir up the gift of God, which is in thee (2 Timothy 1:6).
usage: As an eagle stirreth up her nest (Deuteronomy 32:11) — the nest broken up by the One who means to carry them.
Hatred stirreth up strifes (Proverbs 10:12) — conflict traced to a disposition, not a circumstance.
It stirreth up the dead for thee (Isaiah 14:9) — the grave rousing to meet a fallen king.

etymology: The third-person singular present of strengthen, from strength, Saxon strengthu. Webster 1828: maketh strong; giveth strength or firmness to; confirmeth. Philippians 4:13 makes it the hinge of one of the most quoted and most misquoted verses in Scripture.
biblical_def: Strengtheneth answers the question of where a man’s ability comes from, and Paul’s answer is a Person: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13). The context is not achievement but contentment; Paul has just said he has learned both to be abased and to abound, both to be full and to be hungry, and the all things he can do is the whole range of circumstance he has been given to bear. Ecclesiastes locates a different kind of strength: Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city (Ecclesiastes 7:19) — a wise man in a besieged town outweighs ten captains. The psalmist names an ordinary means through which God gives strength, and does not apologise for its ordinariness: bread which strengtheneth man’s heart (Psalm 104:15). And Proverbs describes the virtuous woman in the language of a labourer: She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms (Proverbs 31:17). The picture across these texts is consistent. Strength is given, not generated; it comes through Christ, through wisdom, through bread, and through work, and in every case the receiving is by God’s appointment.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives STRENGTHENETH as the third person singular of STRENGTHEN: to make strong or stronger; to add strength to, whether physical, moral, or intellectual; to confirm; to establish; to animate or encourage.
webster_full: STRENGTHENETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb STRENGTHEN.
STRENGTHEN, v.t. — To make strong or stronger; to add strength to, either physical or moral.
To confirm; to establish; to fix more firmly; as, to strengthen a resolution or an obligation.
To animate; to encourage; to fix in resolution; as, strengthen thy brethren.
From strength, Saxon strengthu, from strang, strong — the root also of string and strong.
scriptures: Philippians 4:13
I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
Ecclesiastes 7:19
Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city.
Psalm 104:15
And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man's heart.
Proverbs 31:17
She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.
corruption_summary: Philippians 4:13 has been detached from its context and made a promise of achievement — printed on athletic gear and quoted before examinations and business ventures — when Paul wrote it about knowing how to be hungry.
corruption_paragraphs: Read verses 11 and 12 and the misquotation collapses. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content… I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. Then comes verse 13. The all things is that list: hunger, abasement, need, and also plenty, which Paul evidently regarded as the harder of the two to survive. The verse promises sufficiency to endure whatever God assigns, not success in whatever a man attempts. Used the popular way it becomes a charm, and it fails the first believer who prayed it over an outcome God had determined otherwise — which is precisely the man Paul wrote it to comfort.

Psalm 104:15 guards a second and quieter error, the false spirituality that is embarrassed by ordinary means. God gives strength through bread. He gives gladness through wine and dignity through oil, and the psalm lists them among His works of providence without a hint of apology. A piety that expects strength only through extraordinary experience and despises sleep, food, work and the company of the saints is not more spiritual than the psalmist; it is less biblical. Proverbs 31:17 makes the same point from the side of labour: the woman strengthens her arms, and Scripture counts that among her praises rather than against them.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq (H2388), to be strong, to strengthen, to hold fast; amats (H553), to be alert, to make firm; Greek endunamoo (G1743), to empower, to infuse strength; krataioo (G2901), to make mighty.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be or make strong, to seize; behind be strong and of a good courage (Joshua 1:9).
Hebrew amats (H553) — to be alert, to be courageous, to make firm; the constant companion of chazaq in the charge to Joshua.
Greek endunamoo (G1743) — to empower from within; Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13) and be strong in the Lord (Ephesians 6:10).
Greek krataioo (G2901) — to make mighty; strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man (Ephesians 3:16).
Greek sthenoo (G4599) — to make firm; one of the four verbs of 1 Peter 5:10, where God perfects, stablishes, strengthens and settles His people.
usage: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me (Philippians 4:13) — written about knowing how to be hungry.
Wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men (Ecclesiastes 7:19) — one wise man outweighs ten captains.
Bread which strengtheneth man’s heart (Psalm 104:15) — God’s strength through ordinary means.

etymology: The third-person singular present of fade, from Old French fader, to wither, from Latin fatuus in its sense of insipid or faded. Webster 1828: loseth colour or freshness; withereth; declineth. Scripture uses it of grass, flowers, our righteousnesses, and by contrast of what does not fade.
biblical_def: Fadeth is Scripture’s word for the short life of everything under the sun, and it is used to throw the imperishable into relief. Isaiah sets the two next to each other in a verse the New Testament quotes twice: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass (Isaiah 40:7), and the next verse answers, but the word of our God shall stand for ever. The fading is not accidental decay; the breath of the LORD does it. Isaiah applies the same word to the whole created order under judgment: The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish (Isaiah 24:4). James turns it on the rich man specifically, who withers in the middle of his pursuits: the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11). And Peter uses the negative form twice for what God keeps: an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4), and for the faithful elder a crown of glory that fadeth not away (1 Peter 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives FADETH as the third person singular of FADE: to lose colour; to lose freshness or vigour; to wither, as a plant; to decay; to vanish; to perish gradually.
webster_full: FADETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb FADE.
FADE, v.i. — To lose colour; to lose freshness or brightness; to become faint in hue.
To wither, as a plant; to decay; to lose vigour or strength.
To vanish; to disappear gradually; as, the sound or the vision fadeth away.
From Old French fader, allied to Latin vado, to go, and to the English vade, an older form of the same word.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:7
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass.
Isaiah 24:4
The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish.
James 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
1 Peter 1:4
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
1 Peter 5:4
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: A culture organised around the postponement and concealment of decline has no category for Isaiah 40:7, where the fading of human life is not a problem to be solved but the work of God’s own breath, done so that His word may be seen to stand.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah does not say the flower fades because of unfortunate conditions. He says the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it. The transience of human strength, beauty, reputation and life is a divine act with a stated purpose, and the purpose is announced in the next breath: the word of our God shall stand for ever. Against this, the modern project treats ageing as a defect to be corrected, death as a medical failure, and the reminder of either as morbid. The result is not that people fear death less but that they meet it unprepared and alone, having been promised by everything around them that the subject would not come up. Scripture’s counsel is the opposite: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom (Psalm 90:12).

James 1:11 names the specific form the illusion takes for the prosperous: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways — not after his ways, but in the middle of them, with the plans still running. And 1 Peter supplies the only genuine answer, which is not a longer flowering but a different kind of thing altogether: an inheritance that fadeth not away, kept somewhere the moth and the market cannot reach it, and a crown that does not wilt, given by the chief Shepherd to men who shepherded His flock without being lords over it. The believer is not asked to deny that he is grass. He is asked to place his hope in the word that outlasts the grass.
roots_summary: Hebrew nabel (H5034), to wither, to fall away, to fade; yabesh (H3001), to dry up; Greek amarantos (G263), unfading, whence the amaranth flower; maraino (G3133), to wither, to fade away.
roots_lines: Hebrew nabel (H5034) — to fade, to wither, to fall; the flower fadeth (Isaiah 40:7) and we all do fade as a leaf (Isaiah 64:6).
Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up, to wither; the companion verb of nabel in Isaiah’s grass-and-flower figure.
Greek maraino (G3133) — to quench, to wither, to fade away; shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11).
Greek amarantos (G263) — unfading; the inheritance of 1 Peter 1:4, named from a flower the ancients believed never withered.
Greek amarantinos (G262) — of unfading quality; the crown of glory in 1 Peter 5:4.
usage: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth (Isaiah 40:7) — and the reason given is the breath of the LORD.
So also shall the rich man fade away in his ways (James 1:11) — in the middle of his plans, not after them.
An inheritance… that fadeth not away (1 Peter 1:4) — the only answer to the fading is a different kind of thing.

etymology: The third-person singular present of knock, from Saxon cnucian, to strike, to beat. Webster 1828: striketh with something thick or heavy, particularly at a door, for admittance. Its most famous appearance is Revelation 3:20, and its most common misuse is there too.
biblical_def: Knocketh appears at three doors in Scripture, and it matters greatly which door is meant. First, the door of prayer: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened (Matthew 7:8, repeated at Luke 11:10). The three verbs escalate — ask, seek, knock — and the promise is unqualified because the Father who hears is good. Second, the door of the returning Master: ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately (Luke 12:36). The servants are not asked to guess the hour but to be dressed and awake when the knock comes. Third, the door of the Beloved in the Song: I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled (Song of Solomon 5:2) — and the bride, already in bed, delays, and when she opens He is gone. The Song’s picture of a drowsy love that costs a season of communion is the closest Old Testament parallel to the letter to Laodicea.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives KNOCKETH as the third person singular of KNOCK: to strike or beat with something thick or heavy, especially to strike at a door for admittance; to rap. Webster notes the figurative use of seeking entrance or favour.
webster_full: KNOCKETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb KNOCK.
KNOCK, v.i. — To strike or beat with something thick or heavy; to drive or be driven against.
To strike at a door, for admittance; to rap; as, he knocketh at the gate.
Figuratively, to seek entrance, favour, or communication; as in the exhortation, knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
From Saxon cnucian, to knock — probably imitative of the sound, as also in crack and click.
scriptures: Matthew 7:8
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
Luke 11:10
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
Luke 12:36
And ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately.
Song of Solomon 5:2

I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.
corruption_summary: Revelation 3:20 is preached almost universally as an appeal to the unconverted heart, but it is addressed to a church — Laodicea — and the door Christ stands outside is the door of a congregation that has shut Him out of His own assembly.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse reads: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. Every clause before it is addressed to the angel of the church of the Laodiceans, who are lukewarm, self-satisfied, and told to buy gold tried in the fire. The scene is not a sinner’s heart with Christ waiting outside for permission; it is a church that has managed Him out of its own gathering, and the invitation is to any individual within it who will still hear. Read the popular way, the verse teaches that the decisive act is the sinner’s opening, which sits badly with no man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him (John 6:44). Read as written, it is a summons to a compromised congregation, which is a far more searching message and one the modern church needs more.

Matthew 7:8 is sometimes corrupted in the other direction, as though persistent knocking obliged God to grant whatever is asked. The context forbids it: the Lord immediately compares the Father to a human father who gives bread rather than a stone, and a fish rather than a serpent, which means some requests are refused because they are stones and serpents. The Song of Solomon 5 supplies the pastoral warning that fits both texts. The bride hears her Beloved knocking, is comfortable, delays, and opens to an empty threshold; she then walks the city at night looking for Him and is beaten by the watchmen. Delayed response to Christ’s knock costs something real, and Scripture does not soften the account.
roots_summary: Greek krouo (G2925), to knock, to rap at a door; anoigo (G455), to open; Hebrew daphaq (H1849), to beat, to knock; Greek thura (G2374), a door.
roots_lines: Greek krouo (G2925) — to strike, to knock at a door; Matthew 7:8, Luke 12:36, Revelation 3:20.
Greek anoigo (G455) — to open; the passive it shall be opened leaves the opening to God.
Greek thura (G2374) — a door; also used by Christ of Himself, I am the door (John 10:9).
Hebrew daphaq (H1849) — to beat, to knock; the voice of my beloved that knocketh (Song of Solomon 5:2).
Greek aiteo (G154) and zeteo (G2212) — to ask and to seek; the two verbs that stand with krouo in the ascending triad.
usage: To him that knocketh it shall be opened (Matthew 7:8) — the third and most persistent of the three verbs of prayer.
When he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately (Luke 12:36) — servants dressed and awake for an unknown hour.
It is the voice of my beloved that knocketh (Song of Solomon 5:2) — a drowsy love that costs a season of communion.

etymology: The third-person singular present of languish, from Latin languere, to be faint or weak. Webster 1828: becometh faint or feeble; pineth away; loseth strength and animation. In the prophets it is the state of a land under judgment, and it is applied to the ground itself.
biblical_def: Languisheth is what the prophets say of a country that God has struck: it does not merely suffer, it pines. Isaiah pairs it with mourning and puts both on the land itself: The earth mourneth and languisheth: Lebanon is ashamed and hewn down: Sharon is like a wilderness; and Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruits (Isaiah 33:9). The four named places were the fertile glories of the region — the cedars, the plain, the pasture, the vineyard slopes — and each is undone in a single clause. In the great judgment oracle of Isaiah 24 the same verb takes in the whole world: The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish (Isaiah 24:4). Note the order: the earth languishes, and then the haughty people do, so that human pride and the ground under it fall together. Jeremiah reports it of Judah under drought: Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish; they are black unto the ground; and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up (Jeremiah 14:2). And Joel reports it orchard by orchard: The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men (Joel 1:12).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives LANGUISHETH as the third person singular of LANGUISH: to lose strength or animation; to be or become dull, feeble, or spiritless; to pine; to wither, as a plant deprived of moisture.
webster_full: LANGUISHETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb LANGUISH.
LANGUISH, v.i. — To lose strength or animation; to become dull, feeble, or spiritless.
To wither; to fade; to lose the vegetating power, as a plant deprived of moisture.
To pine or waste away; to sink under grief, sickness, or long-continued want.
From Latin langueo, to be faint — the root also of languid, languor, and lax.
scriptures: Isaiah 33:9
The earth mourneth and languisheth: Lebanon is ashamed and hewn down: Sharon is like a wilderness; and Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruits.
Isaiah 24:4
The earth mourneth and fadeth away, the world languisheth and fadeth away, the haughty people of the earth do languish.
Jeremiah 14:2
Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish; they are black unto the ground; and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up.
Joel 1:12

The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men.
corruption_summary: Scripture reads a languishing land as a summons to national repentance, while the modern habit is to read every environmental distress as a purely material problem with purely technical remedies and no moral address at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Joel is the clearest case. The locusts have stripped the country, the vine is dried up, the fig tree languishes, and Joel’s response is not an agricultural programme but a summons: Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the LORD your God, and cry unto the LORD (Joel 1:14). Isaiah 24 states the reason a chapter-length judgment falls on the earth: the earth also is defiled under the inhabitants thereof; because they have transgressed the laws, changed the ordinance, broken the everlasting covenant. The land and the covenant are linked. A generation that can discuss the condition of the ground endlessly and never once ask whether the ordinances have been changed has removed the only cause the prophets ever assign.

The dictionary is equally unwilling to endorse the opposite corruption, in which the land is divinised and man’s dominion over it treated as the original sin. Genesis 1:28 gives the dominion and God calls it good; Psalm 115:16 says the earth hath he given to the children of men. The creation is neither a goddess nor a warehouse. It is a trust that groans under a curse it did not choose (Romans 8:22) and will be delivered when the sons of God are manifested. Isaiah 33:9 shows creation mourning as a witness against the men who defiled it, which is a moral relation, not a merely ecological one — and the answer the prophets give is repentance, followed by the restoration God alone can bring.
roots_summary: Hebrew amal (H535), to be weak, to languish, to droop; abal (H56), to mourn; yabesh (H3001), to dry up, to wither; Greek astheneo (G770), to be weak.
roots_lines: Hebrew amal (H535) — to be feeble, to languish; used of the land, of the gates of Judah, and of the fruitful trees (Isaiah 24:4; Jeremiah 14:2).
Hebrew abal (H56) — to mourn; the constant companion of amal in these oracles, so that the land both mourns and pines.
Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up, to be withered; the vine is dried up (Joel 1:12).
Hebrew umlal (H536) — feeble, languishing; the adjective, have mercy upon me, O LORD; for I am weak (Psalm 6:2).
Greek astheneo (G770) — to be without strength; the New Testament counterpart, used of the sick and of the weak in faith.
usage: The earth mourneth and languisheth (Isaiah 33:9) — the fertile glories of the land undone clause by clause.
The world languisheth… the haughty people of the earth do languish (Isaiah 24:4) — the ground and human pride fall together.
The fig tree languisheth (Joel 1:12) — and Joel’s remedy is a solemn assembly, not a programme.

etymology: The archaic past participle of withhold, from with in its older sense of against or back, and hold. Webster 1828 records withholden alongside withheld. The form survives in the Authorized Version and carries a note of deliberate restraint.
biblical_def: Withholden is used of three things kept back — by God in judgment, by men in cruelty, and by nothing at all from God’s knowledge. God names His own withholding as a summons that failed: And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city (Amos 4:7), and the refrain through that chapter is yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD. The drought was a message, precisely aimed and locally varied so that none could call it chance. Jeremiah traces a withholding to its cause in the people themselves: Your iniquities have turned away these things, and your sins have withholden good things from you (Jeremiah 5:25). Eliphaz uses the word to accuse Job of the cruelty of the comfortable: Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry (Job 22:7) — a charge that was false about Job but describes a real sin. And Job himself uses the word in his final confession, where nothing can be kept back from God: I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives WITHHOLDEN as an old participle of WITHHOLD: held back; restrained; kept back from action, from bestowment, or from use. Webster notes withheld as the more usual modern form.
webster_full: WITHHOLDEN, pp. (old form) — Held back; restrained; kept from proceeding or from being given.
WITHHOLD, v.t. — To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action or from motion.
To retain; to keep back; not to grant; as, to withhold assent, or to withhold bread from the hungry.
To keep from any particular use or from a person who has a claim; hence, to defraud.
From with, in the old sense of against or back, and hold; compare withstand and withdraw.
scriptures: Amos 4:7

And also I have withholden the rain from you, when there were yet three months to the harvest: and I caused it to rain upon one city, and caused it not to rain upon another city: one piece was rained upon, and the piece whereupon it rained not withered.
Jeremiah 5:25
Your iniquities have turned away these things, and your sins have withholden good things from you.
Job 22:7
Thou hast not given water to the weary to drink, and thou hast withholden bread from the hungry.
Job 42:2
I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
corruption_summary: Amos 4:7 says God withheld rain from one city and not another as a deliberate call to repentance, and modern religion has almost entirely lost the category of a providence that is aimed rather than merely arranged.
corruption_paragraphs: The detail in Amos is the point. God did not simply send a drought; He rained on one town and not the next, on one field and not the piece beside it, so that thirsty men walked to a neighbouring city for water and could not tell themselves it was weather. Five times in the chapter God lists a judgment — want of bread, withheld rain, blasting and mildew, pestilence, overthrow — and five times adds yet have ye not returned unto me. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds that God governs all events to His own ends, and Amos 4 shows that some of those ends are legible: a hard providence may be a summons. This must be said carefully, since Job’s friends drew exactly that inference wrongly and were rebuked for it; but the answer to their error is better discernment, not the modern conclusion that providence never addresses anyone.

Job 22:7 preserves their error for our instruction. Eliphaz reasons backward from Job’s suffering to Job’s supposed sin and invents specifics — that he withheld bread from the hungry and water from the weary — which the first chapter has already disproved. The lesson is not that suffering never speaks but that no bystander may assign its meaning to another man. Job 42:2 closes the matter from the other end: no thought can be withholden from thee. God’s purposes cannot be kept back by any creature, and no creature can keep a thought back from Him. That is the ground on which a sufferer may safely leave the interpretation of his affliction with God.
roots_summary: Hebrew mana (H4513), to withhold, to keep back; chasak (H2820), to restrain, to spare; batsar (H1219), to cut off, to restrain; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold back, to restrain.
roots_lines: Hebrew mana (H4513) — to withhold, to keep back; I have withholden the rain from you (Amos 4:7).
Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to restrain, to spare, to hold back; he that spareth his rod hateth his son (Proverbs 13:24).
Hebrew batsar (H1219) — to cut off, to fence in, to restrain; behind no thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2).
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold fast, to hold back; the restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7.
Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, to keep back by fraud; the withheld wages of James 5:4.
usage: I have withholden the rain from you (Amos 4:7) — a drought aimed field by field, so that none could call it chance.
Thy sins have withholden good things from you (Jeremiah 5:25) — the withholding traced to its cause.
No thought can be withholden from thee (Job 42:2) — nothing kept back from God, by any creature.

etymology: The archaic past participle of wax, from Saxon weaxan, to grow, to increase — unrelated to wax the substance. Webster 1828 records it as an old participle of the verb signifying to grow or increase. The word survives in modern English chiefly in wax and wane.
biblical_def: Waxen means grown, and Scripture uses it almost always of a growth that is not good. The cry of Sodom has grown: we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the LORD; and the LORD hath sent us to destroy it (Genesis 19:13) — a city’s sin measured as a noise that reaches heaven and grows until it is answered. Jeremiah applies the word to men who have prospered by injustice: As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich (Jeremiah 5:27), and immediately, They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge (Jeremiah 5:28). The growth is real and so is the shine; the prophet simply refuses to call it blessing. Moses uses the same figure of the nation itself in the Song: But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation (Deuteronomy 32:15). Increase and apostasy are set in a single sentence, in that order.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives WAXEN as an old participle of WAX, to grow: increased; become larger, stronger, or more numerous. Webster distinguishes this verb entirely from wax, the substance produced by bees.
webster_full: WAXEN, pp. (old form) — Grown; increased; become greater in size, number, or degree.
WAX, v.i. — To increase in size; to grow; to become larger; opposed to wane.
To pass from one state to another; to become; as, to wax old, to wax fat, to wax strong.
Not to be confounded with WAX, n., the substance of the honeycomb, which is a distinct word.
From Saxon weaxan, to grow — cognate with the German wachsen and connected with waist in its older sense of growth.
scriptures: Genesis 19:13
For we will destroy this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the LORD; and the LORD hath sent us to destroy it.
Jeremiah 5:27
As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich.
Jeremiah 5:28
They are waxen fat, they shine: yea, they overpass the deeds of the wicked: they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless, yet they prosper; and the right of the needy do they not judge.
Deuteronomy 32:15
But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.
corruption_summary: Prosperity teaching reads increase as the certificate of God’s approval, while Deuteronomy 32:15 and Jeremiah 5:27-28 present growing rich as the ordinary occasion of apostasy and of injustice toward the fatherless.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 32:15 is the whole prosperity gospel answered in one verse. Jeshurun is an affectionate name for Israel, the upright one; the LORD gave him fatness, and the fatness is what he kicked with. The order is exact: waxed fat, then kicked, then forsook God, then lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation. Nothing in the sentence suggests the wealth was withheld or was ill-gotten. God gave it, and the man’s heart did the rest. That is why Agur prayed give me neither poverty nor riches, lest he be full and deny God, or poor and steal. A doctrine that reads increase as a certificate of divine approval has no way to read this verse at all.

Jeremiah 5:27-28 adds the social consequence, and it is specific rather than general. The men are great, rich, fat and shining — and the charge is not that they enjoy their houses but that they judge not the cause, the cause of the fatherless… and the right of the needy do they not judge. The failure is judicial: those with the standing to secure justice for the powerless declined to use it. Scripture’s categories here are the fatherless, the needy, the widow and the stranger — concrete persons with concrete claims — and it holds the prosperous answerable for their cases. Genesis 19:13 completes the picture: a city’s cry grows until it is heard, and then it is answered.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadal (H1431), to grow great; rabah (H7235), to become many; shamen (H8080), to grow fat; Greek auxano (G837), to grow, to increase.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to become great; the cry of them is waxen great (Genesis 19:13).
Hebrew shamen (H8080) — to grow fat, to be sleek; they are waxen fat, they shine (Jeremiah 5:28).
Hebrew rabah (H7235) — to multiply, to become many; used of Israel’s increase in Egypt.
Greek auxano (G837) — to grow, to increase; but grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord (2 Peter 3:18).
Hebrew yeshurun (H3484) — Jeshurun, the upright one; the affectionate name for Israel in Deuteronomy 32:15.
usage: The cry of them is waxen great (Genesis 19:13) — a city’s sin measured as a noise that reaches heaven.
They are become great, and waxen rich (Jeremiah 5:27) — growth the prophet refuses to call blessing.
Thou art waxen fat… then he forsook God (Deuteronomy 32:15) — increase and apostasy in one sentence, in that order.

etymology: The second-person singular past of go, formed on the old past went with the -est ending. Webster 1828 lists it among the forms used with thou. In Scripture it is nearly always used of God going forth for His people, or of His people going after Him.
biblical_def: Wentest is the word of a going-forth remembered, and Scripture uses it for the two goings that matter: God’s out of Seir, and Israel’s after Him into the wilderness. Deborah opens her song with the first: LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water (Judges 5:4). The God of Israel is described as a warrior leaving His camp, and creation reacts. Habakkuk uses the same construction for the whole work of redemption: Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked (Habakkuk 3:13) — a going-forth aimed at a head to be wounded, which reaches back to Genesis 3:15. Jeremiah records the other direction, and it is the tenderest verse in his book: I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown (Jeremiah 2:2). God remembers Israel’s following in the desert as a bride’s devotion, and says so at the head of a chapter of indictment. And in Acts the word is a rebuke turned inside out: Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them (Acts 11:3), the charge against Peter that his account of Cornelius answered for ever.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives WENTEST as the second person singular of the past tense of the verb GO, used with thou: didst go, didst proceed, didst pass from one place or state to another.
webster_full: WENTEST — the second person singular, past tense, of the verb GO; used with the pronoun thou.
WENT — the past tense of GO, borrowed from the obsolete verb WEND, to turn or proceed.
GO, v.i. — To move, to pass, to proceed from one place, condition, or state to another.
To go forth, in Scripture, is often said of God coming out to fight for His people or to execute judgment.
From Saxon wendan, to turn or wend, whence the past went supplied the missing past of go.
scriptures: Judges 5:4
LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir, when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom, the earth trembled, and the heavens dropped, the clouds also dropped water.
Habakkuk 3:13
Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.
Jeremiah 2:2

Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the LORD; I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.
Acts 11:3
Saying, Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them.
corruption_summary: Acts 11:3 records the church’s first attempt to make a cultural boundary into a gospel boundary, and every later version of the same instinct — whichever direction it runs — is answered by the way Peter replied.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge against Peter was not doctrinal in form. Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them — a complaint about table fellowship, which is exactly where such disputes always surface. Peter’s answer is a narrative: the sheet let down, the voice, the three men at the gate, and then the decisive fact, the Holy Ghost fell on them, as on us at the beginning. His conclusion is a question: what was I, that I could withstand God? The apostolic settlement is that God’s giving of the Spirit determines who belongs, and no cultural marker may be added to it. That principle cuts in every direction, against the congregation that would keep out the poorly dressed and the recently converted as firmly as against the party at Jerusalem.

Jeremiah 2:2 supplies the pastoral counterweight, and it is worth dwelling on. God begins a chapter of severe indictment by remembering aloud what Israel was like at first: the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown. He recalls the following before He names the forsaking, and He calls it love. That is how God speaks of a people He is about to charge with two great evils. It is a rebuke to the corrupted pastoral instinct that treats a declining believer’s earlier devotion as evidence it was never real; God does not, and Revelation 2:4 makes the same move with Ephesus — thou hast left thy first love presupposes that the first love was genuine.
roots_summary: Hebrew yatsa (H3318), to go out, to go forth; halak (H1980), to go, to walk; tsaad (H6805), to march, to step; Greek eiserchomai (G1525), to go in, to enter.
roots_lines: Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — to go out, go forth; used of the LORD going out to war (Judges 5:4; Habakkuk 3:13).
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk; when thou wentest after me in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2).
Hebrew tsaad (H6805) — to step, to march; when thou marchedst out of the field of Edom.
Greek eiserchomai (G1525) — to go in, to enter; the charge in Acts 11:3 is that Peter went in.
Hebrew kelulah (H3623) — espousals, betrothal; the love of thine espousals (Jeremiah 2:2).
usage: LORD, when thou wentest out of Seir (Judges 5:4) — God described as a warrior leaving His camp.
Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people (Habakkuk 3:13) — a going-forth aimed at a head to be wounded.
When thou wentest after me in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2) — God remembering a bride’s following before naming her sin.
